presentingComplaint: Increasing breathlessness and confusion over 3 days, brought in from a nursing home by carers.
history: Frail 84-year-old man with severe COPD (GOLD group E, FEV1 32% predicted, on home LTOT 1 L/min via concentrator) and prior exacerbations requiring admission. Carers report progressive breathlessness over 3 days with a change in his usual sputum from clear to green and larger in volume. He has become more drowsy and muddled since yesterday, is eating poorly, and had one episode of not recognising staff. He is not classically 'toxic': he has been only intermittently warm to touch and has not complained of chest pain or overt cough, which is typical of his blunted symptom reporting. Baseline mMRC 4, housebound, uses a rollator. Ex-smoker (60 pack-years, quit 5 years ago). Comorbidities: mild cognitive impairment, osteoporosis, hypertension. Regular inhaled LABA/LAMA/ICS, home nebulised salbutamol, amlodipine. No recent hospitalisation or antibiotics in the last 90 days. No orthopnoea, PND, calf pain or haemoptysis.
examination: Frail, drowsy but rousable elderly man, mildly confused (AMTS 6/10, down from baseline 8). Working hard to breathe with pursed-lip breathing and accessory muscle use. Widespread polyphonic expiratory wheeze with prolonged expiratory phase and quiet breath sounds; scattered coarse crepitations at both bases that shift with coughing. No focal bronchial breathing. Mild bilateral ankle oedema (chronic, unchanged per carers), JVP not raised, no gallop. Warm peripheries, cap refill <2s. Asterixis present (CO2 retention flap). No calf swelling or tenderness.

labs.nt_probnp: 410 pg/mL (near age-adjusted baseline, argues against decompensated heart failure)

imaging: Chest X-ray: hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms and bullae consistent with known emphysema; no new focal consolidation, no lobar collapse, no pneumothorax; heart size normal, no pulmonary oedema or effusions.
microbiology: Sputum sent for Gram stain and culture (purulent, green). Blood cultures sent given fever and confusion. Respiratory viral PCR pending. No prior resistant-organism isolates on record.
differentialDiagnoses: Infective acute exacerbation of COPD with hypercapnic respiratory failure (compensated respiratory acidosis) and CO2-narcosis contributing to confusion
Community-acquired pneumonia (excluded by absence of new consolidation on CXR)
Acute decompensated heart failure / pulmonary oedema (argued against by near-baseline NT-proBNP, no raised JVP, clear CXR)
Pulmonary embolism (no pleuritic pain, unilateral leg findings or unexplained tachycardia/hypoxia disproportionate to CXR)
finalDiagnosis: Infective acute exacerbation of COPD (Anthonisen type 1: increased dyspnoea, increased sputum volume and increased sputum purulence) with acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure in a frail elderly patient; confusion driven by hypercapnia rather than sepsis.
citations: GOLD (Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease) - Management of COPD Exacerbations - 2024
NICE - COPD in over 16s: diagnosis and management (NG115) - 2019
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
stewardship: Anthonisen type 1 exacerbation with purulent sputum plus raised inflammatory markers meets criteria for empirical antibiotics. Start oral/IV amoxicillin-clavulanate (co-amoxiclav) as first-line per GOLD/NICE; use a macrolide or doxycycline if penicillin-allergic. Add controlled oxygen targeting SpO2 88-92% (Venturi 24-28%) to avoid worsening hypercapnia, nebulised bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 40 mg for 5 days), and early consideration of non-invasive ventilation (NIV/BiPAP) for the respiratory acidosis. De-escalate/stop antibiotics per sputum culture and clinical response; total 5-day antibiotic course.
contraindications: Avoid high-flow uncontrolled oxygen - risk of worsening CO2 narcosis in chronic CO2 retainer; titrate to SpO2 88-92%
Penicillin allergy: substitute doxycycline or a macrolide for co-amoxiclav
Caution with systemic corticosteroids given osteoporosis and hyperglycaemia risk; monitor glucose
edgeCases: Confusion in a frail elderly patient may be attributed to sepsis or delirium of another cause; here hypercapnia (PaCO2 61 mmHg) with compensated acidosis is the driver
Low-grade temperature and absent chest pain/cough can mask the diagnosis in frail elders with blunted symptom reporting
If CXR later shows consolidation, reclassify toward pneumonia and broaden accordingly
Failure of NIV or falling GCS mandates escalation discussion consistent with ceiling-of-care and frailty status
expectedMaiK: Infective acute exacerbation of COPD with acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure in a frail elder; treat with controlled oxygen (88-92%), bronchodilators, corticosteroids, empirical co-amoxiclav, and early NIV.
